newsitem.title: ITALY: "Italian Watergate" sparks outrage, spy charges.
newsitem.headline: "Italian Watergate" sparks outrage, spy charges.

text.p: Former premier Silvio Berlusconi's announcement that his Rome headquarters was bugged sparked outrage on Saturday among Italian politicians, some of whom said they were being spied on too.

Rocco Buttiglione, head of a Roman Catholic party allied with Berlusconi, compared the bugging to the Watergate scandal in the United States, which involved spying on political adversaries and led to the resignation of President Richard Nixon in 1974.
"If it turns out that this bug was planted by organs of the state, then we will be faced with a scandal not inferior to Watergate," Buttiglione told reporters.

Berlusconi, head of the centre-right opposition bloc, told a news conference on Friday that a small radio microphone was discovered on Wednesday in a window recess behind his desk in his central Rome headquarters.

"Experts have told me it was in perfect working condition and capable of transmitting across a range of 300 metres," the media tycoon told reporters, holding up a black microphone the size and shape of a cigarette box.

"This is a very serious situation, which is even more serious given that we are dealing with the leader of the opposition," Berlusconi said, adding that he had informed judicial authorities about the discovery.

Leaders across the political spectrum voiced indignation at the news and President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro met Interior Minister Giorgio Napolitano and police chief Fernando Masone. Television said their talks centred on the bugging.
"I think we can definitely say this is a political conspiracy," said Buttiglione, who urged Scalfaro to show a "tough response" to the news. "The atmosphere in Rome is very bad right now," he added.
Some politicians said Berlusconi, premier for seven stormy months in 1994, was not the only one being bugged.
"I think I'm being spied on too, but it doesn't scare me," Post Minister Antonio Maccanico told reporters in Rome.
Secessionist leader Umberto Bossi, whose fiery comments and actions are followed closely by magistrates, said he was no stranger to spying devices.
"We (at the Northern League party) have found, I believe, about nine bugs," Bossi told reporters in Milan.
"What can I say? This is democracy in Italy," he added.

Giuseppe Pisanu, head of Berlusconi's Forza Italia party in the Chamber of Deputies (lower house), said he had asked Napolitano and Prime Minister Romano Prodi to make a formal statement on the "grave and unheard-of matter".
"Last night I also asked (Chamber president Luciano) Violante to call an immediate meeting of the Chamber on the matter," Pisanu told reporters.
Prodi, whose centre-left coalition defeated Berlusconi's conservative alliance in elections last April, told reporters on Friday that he was outraged by the news and would call for an investigation.
Italian magistrates have used hi-tech bugging devices in a number of recent corruption investigations including the latest case involving alleged graft in some state-controlled firms.

Berlusconi is currently standing trial for alleged bribes paid by his Fininvest business empire in return for lenient audits but Justice Minister Giovanni Maria Flick rejected the notion that magistrates were behind the bugging.
"The bugging of a parliamentarian requires authorisation," said Flick, adding that prosecutors would open a probe.
Newspapers entertained a range of other theories on who may have planted the bug, including corrupt members of the secret service or the possibility of industrial espionage.
